# HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning

Sudipta Paul ^(†)^(†)thanks: Equal contribution.    Pengrui
Quan¹¹footnotemark: 1    Aounon Kumar    Nicholas Tzou    Vivek Kulkarni
   Srinivas Chappidi Affiliation: Samsung Research America
Affiliation: {sudipta.paul, pengrui.quan, aounon.kumar, n.tzou,}
Affiliation: {v.kulkarni1, vasu.c}@samsung.com

###### Abstract

Harness optimization, which improves an agent’s prompts, tools, and
workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on
frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the
Darwin–Gödel Machine and the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) rely on
recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where
the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence
being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a
sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints,
break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly
explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation
budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for
budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual
represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context
records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or
regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor
explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of
past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path
child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child
that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that
target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent’s
highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest
baseline by up to $`14.45\%`$ relative improvement in case accuracy
while matching HGM variants’ final performance with
$`2\times`$–$`4\times`$ fewer evaluation budget.

|     |

## 1 Introduction

Agent harness optimization [Khattab et al. (2024)](#bib.bib10);
[Yuksekgonul et al. (2024)](#bib.bib11) improves large language model
(LLM) agents without updating model parameters by optimizing the
prompts, tools, and workflows that govern agent behavior. Recent
self-improving systems [Novikov et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21) automate this
process through evolutionary search. The Darwin–Gödel Machine
(DGM) [Zhang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib1) maintains an archive of agents
and generates new candidates by modifying selected parents, while the
Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) [Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2) selects
candidates based on _clade-metaproductivity_, their potential to produce
strong descendants.

This paradigm is well suited to coding agents because the ability being
improved, understanding and modifying code, also enables
self-modification. Planning tasks, however, require sequences of actions
that satisfy interacting constraints [Zhang et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib7);
[Xie et al. (2024)](#bib.bib18), creating a mismatch that poses two
challenges for existing recursive self-improvement methods.

First, _effective improvement requires a structured context of the
search history_. Planning benchmarks expose a relatively small and
recurring set of constraint failures, so different agents in the search
tree often encounter similar problems. If an editor observes only its
current parent’s evaluation logs, it cannot determine whether a similar
fix has already been attempted elsewhere, whether it improved or
degraded performance, or which previous modifications led to the current
behavior. As a result, different branches may repeatedly rediscover the
same ineffective changes. In HGM’s shopping search, 41.8% of edits
repeat an edit pattern already present in the tree
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
left), with each repeated attempt consuming another full planning
evaluation. What is needed is not simply access to more previous agents,
but explicit _edit–outcome context_: a concise record of what was
changed, what behavior changed as a result, and which changes succeeded,
regressed, or proved ineffective.

Figure 1: Edit behavior in HGM. Among child nodes, 41.8% repeat previous
edits, 19.4% target an error category absent from the parent’s observed
failures, and 64.2% retain the parent’s dominant error category. See
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Edit redundancy ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
for details.

Second, _improvement must be targeted at the specific constraints the
agent violates_. Planning success depends on the correctness of many
interdependent decisions: a single infeasible transfer, invalid coupon,
or unmet product requirement can invalidate an otherwise valid itinerary
or cart. Consequently, a broad modification that improves behavior in
general may still leave the failing case unresolved unless it corrects
the particular constraint violation responsible for failure. Without
explicit guidance, open-ended editing may instead modify an unrelated
harness component or make a diffuse change that does not address the
observed error. In HGM’s shopping search, 19.4% of edits target a
constraint category that the parent never failed
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
middle), and in 64.2% of edits the child retains its parent’s dominant
failure category
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
right). These results suggest that efficient self-improvement for
planning requires both learning from prior edit outcomes and directing
new edits toward the specific constraint failures observed in the
current agent.

We introduce the _Huxley–Gödel Machine Dual_ (HGM-Dual), a
diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient agent harness
evolution. First, it represents agentic evolution as structured
contextual information. This _agent-evolution context_ records what was
changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which attempted
modifications were ineffective. The editor therefore receives explicit
edit–outcome attribution instead of treating previous agent snapshots as
an unstructured archive. This context discourages repeated failures and
allows subsequent edits to build systematically on evidence collected
throughout the search.

Second, HGM-Dual introduces _error-conditioned dual-path child
generation_. For each selected parent, the framework generates
complementary children: a _general child_, which preserves the broad and
open-ended exploration of existing evolutionary methods, and
_specialized children_, which target the harness component most likely
responsible for the parent’s observed errors. The general path retains
the ability to discover unexpected improvements, while the specialized
path provides diagnostic-guided local refinement. Together, the dual
paths balance exploration with targeted exploitation and direct the
evaluation budget toward more informative regions of the harness search
space.

Experiments on travel and shopping planning tasks show that HGM-Dual
outperforms the strongest baseline by up to $`14.45\%`$ relative
improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final
performance with $`2\times`$–$`4\times`$ fewer evaluation budget. These
results demonstrate that structured evolutionary context and diagnostic
guidance can make harness self-improvement both more effective and
substantially more resource-efficient.

## 2 Related Works

Harness Optimization through Self-Improvement. Recent methods improve
frozen LLMs by automatically modifying their agentic harnesses,
including prompts, tools, skills, and workflows [Khattab et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib10); [Opsahl-Ong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12); [Zhang et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib14); [Chen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib15); [Karten et al. (2026)](#bib.bib19); [Lou et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib22). ADAS [Hu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib6), DGM [Zhang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib1), HGM [Wang et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib2), GEPA [Agrawal et al. (2026)](#bib.bib9), and
HyperAgents [Zhang et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib4) search over agent
implementations through iterative or evolutionary self-modification.
Meta-Harness [Lee et al. (2026)](#bib.bib3) gives an agentic proposer
access to the code, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates,
while SkillOpt [Yang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5) optimizes a
natural-language skill through bounded edits and validation.
Collectively, these methods demonstrate that harness optimization can
substantially improve agent performance without updating model
parameters.

Nevertheless, two challenges remain. First, prior edit experience is
either local or excessive: DGM [Zhang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib1) and
HGM [Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2) primarily generate modifications
from the selected parent’s code and evaluation logs, without providing
enough context on the effectiveness of all edits attempted. On the other
hand, archive-based methods [Hu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6); [Lee et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib3); [Lin et al. (2026)](#bib.bib16); [Jiang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17) may flood the evolution context with numerous
previous candidates and raw execution traces. This can obscure useful
edit-outcome relationships and lead to repeated ineffective
modifications across the search tree. Second, although prior methods
guide candidate selection or validation [Yang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib5);
[Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2); [Zhang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib1);
[Zhang et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib4), edit generation itself remains
largely open-ended and may not target the harness component responsible
for observed failures. Such weakly targeted exploration can require
substantial evaluation resources. HGM-Dual addresses these limitations
by maintaining a concise, structured agent-evolution context and by
generating both a general child for broad exploration and an
error-conditioned specialized child for targeted refinement.

## 3 HGM-Dual

### 3.1 Problem Setup

Agent Harness Optimization. We consider a frozen language model whose
behavior is controlled by an agent harness

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{W}),
       ```                                                 |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$ specifies the prompt and instructions provided to
the model, $`\mathcal{T}`$ denotes the set of available tools, and
$`\mathcal{W}`$ defines the agentic workflow that governs how the model
and tools interact to solve a task. The parameters of the underlying
language model remain fixed throughout optimization; only the components
of $`\mathcal{H}`$ are modified.

Given a task $`x`$ sampled from a task distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$,
executing the frozen language model under harness $`\mathcal{H}`$
produces an output $`\mathcal{H}(x)`$. We evaluate this output using a
task-specific scoring function $`J(x,\mathcal{H}(x))`$, which measures
the quality of the harness execution on task $`x`$. Agent harness
optimization seeks a harness that maximizes expected performance over
the task distribution:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{H}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[J\!\left(x,\mathcal{H}(x)\right)\right].
``` |  | (2) |

### 3.2 Overview

![Refer to caption](2610.30042v1/Picture3.png)

Figure 2: HGM search: select a parent, generate an open-ended edit,
evaluate the child, and add it to the archive.

#### HGM.

HGM optimizes an agent harness through evolutionary self-modification.
Starting from an initial harness $`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$, HGM maintains an
archive $`\mathcal{A}`$ of previously evaluated harnesses organized as
an evolutionary tree
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Overview ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")).
Each node corresponds to a harness, and each edge corresponds to a
modification that produces a child from its parent. At each iteration,
HGM selects a parent harness $`\mathcal{H}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}`$ using its
*clade-metaproductivity* criterion, which is designed to favor
candidates with the potential to produce strong descendants. An editor
then examines the selected harness and its evaluation feedback, proposes
an open-ended modification, evaluates the resulting child, and adds it
to the archive. The editor primarily conditions on the selected harness
and its current evaluation context $`\varepsilon_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i}\right).
``` |  | (3) |

Thus, the archive records an evolutionary history, but that history is
not explicitly represented as structured edit-outcome evidence for the
editor. Moreover, because the edit is open-ended, it is not explicitly
constrained to address the failures observed in the selected parent.

![Refer to caption](2610.30042v1/Picture1.png)

Figure 3: Overview of HGM-Dual and one expansion round. Given a selected
parent $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$, HGM-Dual constructs an evolution context
$`\mathcal{Z}_{i}`$ by summarizing edits and outcomes along its
ancestral path $`\mathrm{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})`$. The evolution context
is provided to both editing paths: a general editor proposes an
open-ended improvement, while specialized editors target the
highest-ranked errors in the parent’s error profile $`\varepsilon_{i}`$.
The resulting children are evaluated under the same protocol, and only
the strongest child is added to the archive.

#### HGM-Dual.

HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary search procedure but changes how
each selected parent is expanded (we refer readers to Section
[A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Full HGM-Dual ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
for full integration). As illustrated in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ HGM. ‣ 3.2 Overview ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
it introduces two mechanisms. First, rather than conditioning an edit
only on the selected harness $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$ and its evaluation
context $`\varepsilon_{i}`$, HGM-Dual additionally provides an evolution
context $`\mathcal{Z}_{i}`$ that summarizes the edits and outcomes along
its ancestral lineage:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i},\mathcal{Z}_{i}\right).
``` |  | (4) |

Second, HGM-Dual augments HGM’s open-ended child generation with
error-conditioned editing. Each expansion generates both general and
error-conditioned children. Thus, HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary
backbone while making edit generation both *history-aware* and
*error-aware*. We summarize the HGM-Dual expansion process in Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
and describe them in
Sections [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
and [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Error-Conditioned Dual-Path Child Generation ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
respectively.

### 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context

An editor observing only the current harness and its evaluation feedback
cannot reliably attribute performance changes to prior edits or identify
previously failed modifications. Providing the full archive and raw
traces would address this limitation but is costly and difficult to
interpret. HGM-Dual therefore compresses the relevant evolutionary
history into a structured context.

For each non-root harness $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$ with parent
$`\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}}`$, we define an evolution record

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\zeta_{i}=\left(d_{i},\,u_{i},\,\Delta\widehat{J}_{i},\,\Delta\mathbf{f}_{i},\,b_{i}\right),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`d_{i}`$ summarizes the edit, $`u_{i}`$ records functionality
added, removed, or invoked,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\widehat{J}_{i}=\widehat{J}(\mathcal{H}_{i})-\widehat{J}(\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}}),
``` |  | (6) |

measures its performance impact, and

|     |                                                        |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta\mathbf{f}_{i}=\mathbf{f}_{i}-\mathbf{f}_{p_{i}}
       ```                                                     |     | (7) |

captures changes in constraint-level errors. Finally, $`b_{i}`$
summarizes the observed behavioral consequences. Thus, $`\zeta_{i}`$
links each modification to its functional, performance, and behavioral
effects.

Let
$`\operatorname{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})=(\mathcal{H}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{H}_{p_{i}},\mathcal{H}_{i})`$
denote the ordered ancestral path to $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$. We define its
lineage context as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{Z}_{i}=\operatorname{Summarize}\left(\left\{\zeta_{j}:\mathcal{H}_{j}\in\operatorname{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i})\right\}\right).
``` |  | (8) |

This bounded summary preserves which functionality was introduced and
used, which edits produced improvements or regressions, and how behavior
evolved along the lineage, while consolidating redundant records.

When expanding $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$, the editor receives its source,
current evaluation context $`\varepsilon_{i}`$, and lineage context
$`\mathcal{Z}_{i}`$. This compact memory helps avoid repeating failed
changes, retain complementary improvements, and identify interactions
between edits that are not apparent from the current score alone.

Algorithm 1 HGM-Dual Expansion

### 3.4 Error-Conditioned Dual-Path Child Generation

The space of possible modifications to $`\mathcal{P}`$, $`\mathcal{T}`$,
and $`\mathcal{W}`$ is large, and unrestricted generation frequently
produces plausible but irrelevant edits. HGM-Dual therefore uses two
complementary editing paths: a general path for broad exploration and an
error-conditioned path for targeting verified weaknesses. To avoid
specializing to noisy failure signals, the error-conditioned path is
enabled only when a one-time pre-search test shows sufficient task-level
agreement ($`\kappa\geq 0.4`$) and dominant-category stability
($`\rho_{B}\geq 0.7`$); otherwise, expansion uses only the general path.

For a selected harness $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$, let

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\varepsilon_{i}=\left(J(\mathcal{H}_{i}),\mathbf{f}_{i},\mathcal{S}_{i}\right),\qquad\mathbf{f}_{i}=\left(f_{i,c}\right)_{c\in\mathcal{C}},
``` |  | (9) |

denote its evaluation context, where $`J(\mathcal{H}_{i})`$ is its
evaluation score, $`\mathbf{f}_{i}`$ is the vector of evaluator-category
error frequencies, $`\mathcal{C}`$ is the set of evaluator-defined error
categories, and $`\mathcal{S}_{i}`$ contains representative execution
traces and evaluator feedback. The general child is produced by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{gen}}_{i}=\operatorname{Edit}_{\mathrm{gen}}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i};\varepsilon_{i},\mathcal{Z}_{i}\right).
``` |  | (10) |

This editor may modify any harness component and is instructed to
identify a broadly useful improvement from the task specification,
current behavior, and evolutionary history. It therefore preserves the
open-ended character of evolutionary search and can discover changes
that are not associated with a single evaluator-defined failure.

For the specialized path, HGM-Dual selects two target errors from the
observed error profile of $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$. The two target error
categories are selected as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{i,k}^{*}=\operatorname{TopK}_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\left(f_{i,c},\,k\right),\qquad k\in\{1,2\},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`f_{i,c}`$ denotes the measured frequency of error category $`c`$
for $`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$. Here, $`c_{i,1}^{*}`$ and $`c_{i,2}^{*}`$
denote the first- and second-highest-ranked error categories,
respectively.

For each selected target error, an error-conditioned child is generated
as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{err}}_{i,k}=\operatorname{Edit}_{\mathrm{err}}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i};c_{i,k}^{*},\mathcal{S}_{i}^{c_{i,k}^{*}},\mathcal{Z}_{i}\right),\qquad k\in\{1,2\},
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\mathcal{S}_{i}^{c_{i,k}^{*}}`$ contains the traces and
evaluator feedback associated with target error $`c_{i,k}^{*}`$. For
each target, the specialized editor is asked to diagnose the
corresponding failure, identify the responsible prompt, tool, or
workflow behavior, and propose a focused correction while preserving
capabilities that are already successful.

All three children are executed on the same optimization set and
evaluated with the same reward function $`\widehat{J}`$. HGM-Dual
retains

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{+}_{i}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}\in\left\{\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{gen}}_{i},\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{err}}_{i,1},\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{err}}_{i,2}\right\}}\widehat{J}(\mathcal{H}).
``` |  | (13) |

The best child, its evaluation context, and edit attribution relative to
$`\mathcal{H}_{i}`$ are added to the archive; the others are discarded.
This dual-path procedure balances exploration and exploitation: the
general child enables broad improvements, while specialized children
target prominent failures. Retaining only the best child limits archive
growth and focuses the search budget on promising harnesses.

## 4 Experiments

| HGM | 4000 | 77.06 $`\pm`$ 0.53 | 30.42 | 83.12 $`\pm`$ 0.27 | 50.83 |
| HGM-CA | 4000 | 83.23 $`\pm`$ 2.65 | 54.17 | 85.32 $`\pm`$ 0.90 | 58.33 |
| HGM-CF | 4000 | 84.11 $`\pm`$ 0.07 | 56.25 | 86.67 $`\pm`$ 1.99 | 60.83 |

Table 1: Performance comparison of task agent optimization for Travel
and Shopping at an evaluation budget of 4000. Best per column in bold,
second best underlined.

Benchmark. We evaluate HGM-Dual on the *DeepPlanning* benchmark [Zhang
et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib7), which consists of two constrained
long-horizon planning tasks: travel planning and shopping. Both require
maintaining global consistency across many interdependent decisions
while satisfying numerous explicit and implicit constraints. In travel
planning, the agent uses nine APIs to construct minute-level itineraries
of up to seven days, evaluated by 21 feasibility checks across eight
dimensions such as temporal, spatial, and budget consistency. In
shopping, the agent searches an average of 171 records through 15 APIs
over 45 product and user attributes, while jointly selecting products
and coupons subject to product, eligibility, threshold, stacking,
delivery, and budget constraints. These interacting constraints make
locally valid decisions insufficient: the agent must ensure that the
complete itinerary or cart remains globally feasible.

Evaluation Metrics. We assess each method along two dimensions. a) *task
performance*: For travel, we report a composite score that measures
overall constraint satisfaction and case accuracy that measures the
proportion of fully correct cases. For shopping, we report a match score
that measures how many ground-truth products are correctly selected and
case accuracy that measures exact cart-level matches. b) *Compute
efficiency*: Following HGM, we define the evaluation budget as the
number of plans generated during optimization and apply this measure
consistently to HGM, HGM variants, and HGM-Dual.

Experimental Setup. The optimization process starts from an initial
harness of the task agent (seed agent) with a simple multi-turn loop, a
minimal task prompt, and access to the task-specific tools of the
benchmark. The agent editor is an LLM agent that updates the harness
components (e.g., prompt, workflow, tool, verifier) of the task agent.
The objective is to obtain the best-performing task agent by optimizing
the harness alone; the underlying model weights are never updated.
Information (e.g., code, logs, failing traces) supplied to the editor is
gathered deterministically by a fixed procedure rather than through
agentic exploration. For both travel planning and shopping tasks, we
optimize on $`60`$ samples and evaluate on $`120`$ samples ($`60`$
unseen samples), so that generalization beyond the optimization set is
measured explicitly. Unless otherwise specified, the agent editor uses
GPT-5.4 (reasoning effort medium) and the task agent uses GPT-5.4-mini
(reasoning effort high).

#### Error Categorization.

Error categories are produced by a deterministic, rule-based
categorizer, one per domain. In travel, the categories follow the
benchmark’s evaluator: each of its eight commonsense dimensions (e.g.,
time feasibility, business hours) is a category, and violated hard
constraints from the query are grouped by the entity they concern
(flight, train, hotel, restaurant, attraction, or budget). Shopping
considers four product level error categories (missing product, unmet
feature, user-profile mismatch, not cheapest) and three cart level error
categories (budget, cart not cheapest, coupon).

Baselines. We compare HGM-Dual against ADAS [Hu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib6), GEPA [Agrawal et al. (2026)](#bib.bib9), HGM [Wang
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2), HGM-Customized (Agentic Editor)
(HGM-CA) [Zhang et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib4), and HGM-Customized (Fixed
Context Editor) (HGM-CF). ADAS and GEPA are two LLM driven optimization
process to improve agentic system performance, while HGM is a
self-referential improvement algorithm in which a task agent edits its
own implementation. Since our setting requires non-coding, long-horizon
planning, we also consider HGM-CA (HGM-Customized (Agentic Editor)), a
domain-customized variant of HGM. HGM-CA augments the original framework
with domain-specific editing mechanisms designed to adapt the agent’s
prompts, tools, and workflow behavior to the planning setting. In this
setting, the editor has agentic access with bash and file read/write
tools to navigate task agents source code and logs. Similar to
HGM-Dual’s agent editor setting, we also consider HGM-CF (HGM-Customized
(Fixed Context Editor)). In this setting, task agents code and logs are
gathered deterministically and provided in the context of the agent
editor to generate edits. HGM-CF gives HGM the same interface used by
HGM-Dual, isolating the effect of agent evolution context and
error-conditioned child generation. We do not compare with DGM [Zhang et
al. (2026b)](#bib.bib1) because HGM has previously been shown to
outperform DGM in both task performance and improvement-budget
efficiency.

Figure 4: Budget efficiency and error breakdown. (a, b) Best agent
performance on {1k, 2k, 3k, 4k} evaluation budgets for travel and
shopping task. (c, d) Per-category change in failure rate of the best
agent after optimization relative to the seed agent on the $`60`$
held-out task instances. Right-hand column gives the seed agent’s
failure rate, filled markers denote $`q<0.05`$.

### 4.1 Evaluation

Performance Comparison to Baseline Approaches.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
reports the performance comparison to baselines (HGM, HGM-CA, HGM-CF) at
$`4000`$ evaluation budget. Vanilla HGM barely moves beyond the seed
harness on either domain, gaining only $`0.60`$ composite points on
travel and $`1.21`$ on shopping, and leaving shopping case accuracy
unchanged at $`50.83`$. This confirms that an editor designed for coding
benchmarks transfers poorly to long-horizon planning, and motivates the
customized variants. HGM-CF the strongest baseline on all four metrics
($`84.11`$ and $`86.67`$ composite, $`56.25`$ and $`60.83`$ case
accuracy). HGM-Dual attains the best result on every metric in both
domains, improving over HGM-CF by $`3.66`$ and $`2.56`$ composite points
and by $`8.13`$ and $`5.84`$ case accuracy points on travel and
shopping, respectively. Notably, the margin is consistently larger in
case accuracy than in composite score, indicating that HGM-Dual does not
merely accumulate partial credit across checkpoints but converts a
larger fraction of plans into fully constraint-satisfying solutions

Budget Efficiency. We have analyzed the budget efficiency of HGM-Dual by
evaluating the performance of selected best agents at different
evaluation budget steps. We have considered selecting best agents at 1k,
2k, 3k and 4k evaluations and evaluate it on all $`120`$ instances for
both travel and shopping task
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(a,b)).
On travel
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(a)),
HGM-CF is slightly ahead at 1k ($`84.9`$ vs. $`83.8`$) but then stalls.
HGM-CF returns the same agent at 1k, 2k and 3k and ends at $`84.1`$.
HGM-Dual, in contrast, improves at every checkpoint, overtakes HGM-CF at
2k ($`85.7`$) and reaches $`87.8`$ at 4k. On shopping
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(b)),
HGM-Dual makes most of its gain within the first 1k evaluations, rising
from $`81.9`$ to $`90.4`$, and stays near that level through 4k
($`89.2`$), whereas HGM-CF improves gradually and ends at $`86.7`$. The
domain-customized variant HGM-CA remains below both methods across the
budget range on travel and below HGM-Dual throughout on shopping.
Overall, HGM-Dual converts the evaluation budget into performance far
more efficiently than HGM-CF: it either keeps improving where HGM-CF
plateaus (travel) or reaches HGM-CF’s final score using roughly a
quarter of the budget (shopping). Note that HGM-Dual’s rejected child’s
evaluation is also counted towards the total evaluation budget used.

Error Profile Analysis. To identify the source of these gains, we
decompose the failures of HGM-Dual and HGM-CF’s final agent ($`4`$k
budget) on the $`60`$ held-out task instances
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(c,d)).
Each row is an evaluator-defined error category, and each marker gives a
method’s change in the fraction of tasks failing that category relative
to the seed agent; negative values indicate fewer errors. The right-hand
column reports the seed agent’s own failure rate. Rows are grouped into
commonsense-quality and hard-constraint errors for travel and into
product- and cart-level errors for shopping. Categories failed by the
seed agent on fewer than $`5\%`$ of tasks are omitted, filled markers
denote statistically significant changes, and the bottom panels report
the share of tasks with any error. On travel
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(c)),
both methods eliminate most time feasibility and itinerary structure
errors, the two most frequent categories. However, HGM-Dual is the only
method that also removes route consistency errors (from $`16.7\%`$ of
tasks to $`1.7\%`$, versus $`10.0\%`$ for HGM-CF) and sandbox compliance
errors (from $`10.0\%`$ to $`2.5\%`$, versus $`8.3\%`$), and it reduces
the share of tasks with any error from $`73.3\%`$ to $`34.6\%`$,
compared with $`47.5\%`$ for HGM-CF. On shopping
(Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Error Categorization. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")(d)),
the gap is concentrated in the most frequent category, unmet features:
HGM-Dual more than halves it (from $`24.2\%`$ to $`10.8\%`$) whereas
HGM-CF leaves it essentially unchanged ($`20.8\%`$). *The advantage of
HGM-Dual therefore stems more from resolving frequently appearing
failure modes that HGM-CF leaves untouched.*

Performance Comparison at Low Budget Regime. Due to the high cost of
long-horizon agent evaluation and performance plateau, we evaluate ADAS
and GEPA only at $`1000`$ evaluations.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
reports the low-budget regime performance for different baselines. The
two non-evolutionary optimizers improve over the Seed Agent on travel
($`80.83`$ and $`81.67`$ composite) but are essentially flat on
shopping, where GEPA in fact falls below the seed harness in both
metrics. Vanilla HGM is similarly ineffective at this budget. On Travel,
the customized variant HGM-CF is the strongest method ($`84.90`$
composite, $`47.50`$ case accuracy), with HGM-Dual being second highest.
On shopping, HGM-Dual dominates every baseline by a wide margin,
reaching $`90.35`$ composite and $`70.83`$ case accuracy and exceeding
the strongest competing method by $`5.89`$ and $`14.16`$ points
respectively.

#### Impact of Agent Evolution Context.

We analyze and compare the edits made by two variants of HGM runs:
HGM-CF and HGM-CF + Agent Evolution Context (no error-conditioned child
generation). For each edit/expansion, we record its outcome against its
parent on the cases both were evaluated on, its source diff, and the
redundancy of its stated goal, measured as the maximum TF-IDF cosine
against the goals of its ancestors.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Impact of Error Conditioning. ‣ 4.1 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
shows that the Agent Evolution Context makes edits less redundant within
a lineage ($`0.22\rightarrow 0.17`$). Edits are less destructive: they
worsen fewer instances ($`37.6\%\rightarrow 31.9\%`$). Most importantly,
adding Agent Evolution Context in the editor improves child agent’s
performance compared to their parent more often
($`31.3\%\rightarrow 41.0\%`$). Therefore, the Agent Evolution Context
alters the proposal distribution of the self-improvement steps
positively rather than only improving the final score.

#### Impact of Error Conditioning.

We ablate error conditioning from HGM-Dual. In the ablated setting, the
error-conditioned child agent generation prompt omits the error category
but everything else remain the same as HGM-Dual (number of total
children agents generated per expand, sequence of generation, and best
of the child agent selection). At an evaluation budget of $`1000`$, the
ablation scores 87.68 vs. 90.35 for HGM-Dual
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Impact of Error Conditioning. ‣ 4.1 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"))
attributing $`~2\%`$ improvement on the error conditioning. Our error
analysis also show that error-conditioning results in resolving
frequently appearing failure modes.
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Impact of Error Conditioning. ‣ 4.1 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
also shows adding evolution context on top HGM-CF boosts performance.
Adding error conditional generation on top of HGM-CF + evolution context
further improves performance.

|----|----|----|
| Improves on its parent (%) $`\uparrow`$ | 31.3 | 41.0 |
| Common instances made worse (%) $`\downarrow`$ | 37.6 | 31.9 |
| Goal repeats from its lineage $`\downarrow`$ | 0.22 | 0.17 |

Generalization Across Task Models. To evaluate whether HGM-Dual
generalizes across LLMs for task agent, we further conduct experiments
with Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B [Mistral AI (2026)](#bib.bib8). In this
setup, we still use GPT-5.4 (reasoning medium) for agent editor. As
shown in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Impact of Error Conditioning. ‣ 4.1 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
harness optimization improves the composite score for
Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B, although its effect on case accuracy is
limited. Standard HGM-CF provides only a modest increase in composite
score, from $`32`$ to $`34`$, and reduces case accuracy from $`1.6\%`$
to $`0.8\%`$. In contrast, HGM-Dual raises the composite score to
$`42`$, outperforming the seed agent and HGM-CF by $`10`$ and $`8`$
points, respectively, while retaining the seed agent’s case accuracy of
$`1.6\%`$.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for efficient
agent harness optimization. By incorporating structured agent-evolution
context, HGM-Dual enables the editor to learn from prior edit outcomes
and avoid redundant or ineffective modifications. Its error-conditioned
dual-path generation further combines open-ended exploration with
targeted refinement of error-relevant harness components. Experiments on
travel and shopping planning tasks demonstrate that these complementary
mechanisms outperform strong self-improving baselines while
substantially reducing the required evaluation budget. Our ablations
further show that evolution context provides consistent performance
gains, whereas dual-path generation accelerates improvement under
constrained budgets. Together, these results demonstrate that explicitly
modeling evolutionary history and balancing general with error-targeted
search can make agent harness evolution more effective and
resource-efficient. Future work may extend the evolution context beyond
individual lineages to share useful edit-outcome evidence across the
entire search tree. Future work could jointly learn an evolving context
and dual-path manager to adapt evidence selection, editing strategies,
and resource allocation throughout the search. Finally, evaluating
HGM-Dual across broader task domains and online environments would help
characterize the transferability and long-term robustness of the evolved
harnesses.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Edit redundancy

#### Edit-redundancy calculation for the shopping task.

We analyze every non-root edit proposal in the search-tree archives of
the shopping task, yielding $`N_{\mathrm{HGM}}=67`$ proposals and
$`N_{\mathrm{Dual}}=51`$ proposals.

Each proposal is tagged using the following seven error categories:

1.  1.
    Coupon correctness: selecting, validating, or applying coupons
    correctly;
2.  2.
    Profile compliance: satisfying user-profile requirements such as
    gender or size;
3.  3.
    Shipping constraints: satisfying destination and delivery-time
    requirements;
4.  4.
    Budget compliance: respecting minimum or maximum spending
    constraints;
5.  5.
    Cart completeness: including all requested items and excluding
    unwanted items;
6.  6.
    Exact feature matching: satisfying explicit product attributes such
    as brand, color, season, rating, or review distribution; and
7.  7.
    Price optimality: selecting the cheapest valid products.

The tags are determined from each proposal’s optimization goal and
proposed changes using the same rules for both methods. Because an edit
can address multiple errors, the categories are not mutually exclusive.
We represent each proposal by the exact combination of its assigned
categories, which we refer to as its *edit pattern*. For example,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\text{profile compliance},\,\text{shipping constraints},\,\text{exact feature matching},\,\text{price optimality})
``` |  |

is one edit pattern, whereas

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (\text{shipping constraints},\,\text{exact feature matching})
       ```                                                            |     |

is another. Two proposals are considered to have the same edit pattern
only when their complete sets of error categories are identical.

For method $`m`$, let $`n_{m}(s)`$ be the number of proposals assigned
to edit pattern $`s`$. Its share of the tree archive is

|     |                                           |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{m}(s)=100\times\frac{n_{m}(s)}{N_{m}}.
       ```                                        |     | (14) |

The edit patterns are ranked independently for HGM and HGM-Dual in
descending order of $`n_{m}(s)`$. The figure reports the share of
repeated edit pattern above.

### A.2 Edit-targeting mismatch

We treat each non-initial candidate as an edit and compare it with the
candidate from which it was derived. Each edit’s stated objective and
proposed changes are mapped to functional error categories, using labels
mentioned in Section
[A.1](#A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Edit-redundancy calculation for the shopping task. ‣ A.1 Edit redundancy ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning").

An edit is classified as having *no corresponding parent error category*
when it targets at least one functional component for which no error was
reported in its parent. The metric is the fraction of edits satisfying
this condition. The *dominant error category* is the category associated
with the largest number of failing evaluation cases.

### A.3 Estimated Cost

As shown in
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.3 Estimated Cost ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning"),
evaluating long-horizon planning agents is computationally expensive,
particularly after harness optimization, where 1k case evaluations can
cost hundreds of dollars in task-agent API usage. Given this cost, we
prioritize the available evaluation budget toward independent runs of
the HGM variants, which are the primary focus of our study. We therefore
evaluate ADAS and GEPA at the 1k budget as reference baselines, while
reserving the more expensive 4k experiments for HGM, HGM variants, and
HGM-Dual.

|          | Unoptimized | Optimized   |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| Travel   | \$400–800   | \$520–1,010 |
| Shopping | \$140–360   | \$300–910   |

Table 6: Estimated task-agent API cost (USD) of 1000 samples evaluations
on Travel and Shopping. The task agent is GPT-5.4-mini (high reasoning
effort). Optimized averaged candidate agents evaluated by HGM and
HGM-Dual. Lower bounds assume $`{\sim}80\%`$ of input tokens are served
from the prompt cache; upper bounds assume no caching.

### A.4 Full HGM-Dual

Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ A.4 Full HGM-Dual ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
summarizes the complete procedure. HGM-Dual keeps the search loop of
HGM ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)): at each iteration, it either
*expands* the archive by modifying a selected parent or *evaluates* an
existing harness on one additional task. Both choices are made by
Thompson sampling, and at the end of the search the harness with the
highest posterior success rate is returned. The only change is in the
expansion step. Instead of producing a single open-ended modification,
HGM-Dual calls Expand
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")),
which builds the evolution context from the parent’s lineage
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")),
generates one general and two error-conditioned children
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Error-Conditioned Dual-Path Child Generation ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")),
and adds only the strongest child to the archive.

The symbols in
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ A.4 Full HGM-Dual ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")
are as follows. For each harness $`\mathcal{H}`$,
$`n_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})`$ and
$`n_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H})`$ count its passed and failed
evaluation tasks, while $`n^{C}_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})`$ and
$`n^{C}_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H})`$ aggregate these counts over
its clade, i.e., the subtree rooted at $`\mathcal{H}`$. The clade counts
measure how productive the descendants of $`\mathcal{H}`$ have been and
guide parent selection. The individual counts measure the harness’s own
performance and guide evaluation and final selection. $`N_{t}`$ is the
number of evaluations spent so far. The archive is expanded when
$`|\mathcal{A}|\leq N_{t}^{\alpha}`$, where $`\alpha\in[0,1]`$ controls
how quickly the tree widens relative to the evaluation budget. $`\tau`$
is a scheduler that increases over the search. It sharpens the sampled
Beta distributions over time, shifting the search from exploration
toward exploitation. $`S^{C}(\mathcal{H})`$ and $`S(\mathcal{H})`$ are
the Thompson samples drawn from the clade-level and individual Beta
posteriors, used to select the parent to expand and the harness to
evaluate, respectively. Finally, $`I_{\rho}`$ is the $`\rho`$-percentile
of a harness’s Beta posterior. Returning the harness that maximizes it
favors candidates whose high success rate is supported by sufficient
evaluations.

0:  Initial harness $`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$, widening parameter $`\alpha`$,
scheduler $`\tau`$, percentile $`\rho`$ for final selection, error
categories $`\mathcal{C}`$ with weights $`w_{c}`$.

1:  Initialize archive $`\mathcal{A}`$ as a tree with root
$`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$

2:  Evaluate $`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$ and construct its evaluation context
$`\varepsilon_{0}`$

3:  Initialize counters $`n^{C}_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})`$,
$`n^{C}_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H})`$,
$`n_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})`$,
$`n_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H})`$ for all
$`\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{A}`$

4:  while evaluation budget is not exhausted do

5:   if $`|\mathcal{A}|\leq N_{t}^{\alpha}`$ and expandable parents
exist then

6:    Expand:

7:    for each $`\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{A}`$ do

8:     Sample
$`S^{C}(\mathcal{H})\sim\mathrm{Beta}\big(\tau(1+n^{C}_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})),\,\tau(1+n^{C}_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H}))\big)`$

9:    end for

10:    Select parent
$`\mathcal{H}_{i}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}}S^{C}(\mathcal{H})`$

11:
   $`(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{H}_{i}^{+})\leftarrow\textsc{Expand}(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i},\mathcal{A})`$
$`\triangleright`$
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context ‣ 3 HGM-Dual ‣ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning")

12:    Update $`n_{\mathrm{success}},n_{\mathrm{failure}}`$ for
$`\mathcal{H}_{i}^{+}`$ from its selection evaluations

13:    Update $`n^{C}_{\mathrm{success}},n^{C}_{\mathrm{failure}}`$ for
$`\mathcal{H}_{i}^{+}`$ and its ancestors

14:   else

15:    Evaluate:

16:    for each $`\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{A}`$ with remaining tasks do

17:     Sample
$`S(\mathcal{H})\sim\mathrm{Beta}\big(\tau(1+n_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H})),\,\tau(1+n_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H}))\big)`$

18:    end for

19:    Select harness
$`\mathcal{H}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}}S(\mathcal{H})`$

20:    Allocate a task to $`\mathcal{H}^{\star}`$ and update its
evaluation context $`\varepsilon^{\star}`$

21:    Update $`n_{\mathrm{success}},n_{\mathrm{failure}}`$ for
$`\mathcal{H}^{\star}`$

22:    Update $`n^{C}_{\mathrm{success}},n^{C}_{\mathrm{failure}}`$ for
$`\mathcal{H}^{\star}`$ and its ancestors

23:   end if

24:  end while

25:  return
$`\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}\in\mathcal{A}}I_{\rho}\big(1+n_{\mathrm{success}}(\mathcal{H}),\,1+n_{\mathrm{failure}}(\mathcal{H})\big)`$

Algorithm 2 Huxley–Gödel Machine Dual (HGM-Dual)
